story.text: A frog the length of a thumb — yellow, black-blotched, awake by day — once sat on mossy rocks by the mountain streams of west-central Panama.
Its skin carries zetekitoxin, a poison named for the frog itself and the most potent in its family.
It has no eardrums, so beside loud water it waves: a male slowly rotates a forelimb to claim a rock or court a female.
Then the chytrid fungus Bd, which invades amphibian skin, swept through Panama and reached El Valle de Antón, the last stronghold, in the mid-2000s.
No one has recorded one in the wild since 2009.
Maryland Zoo bred the first in human care; over 1,000 adults now live at more than 50 North American institutions, with colonies in El Valle and Gamboa.
Panama made it an ecological and cultural symbol by law in 2010; every August 14, El Valle's schoolchildren parade as frogs.
Protective skin bacteria, even a genetically engineered strain, have not yet shielded it from Bd.
So in 2025 the rescue project set 100 captive-bred frogs in mesh pens near El Valle; about 70 percent died of chytrid in twelve weeks, and the survivors were released.
To witness the Panamanian golden frog is to watch a national symbol wave from behind glass — and wait for word from the stream.

reproduction.text: From November to January a male clasps a female and she lays one long strand of eggs on rock in a shallow stream; tadpoles hatch in about nine days, cling to the stone with a belly sucker, and take six to seven months to become frogs.

insight.text: One frog's skin holds enough toxin to kill 1,200 mice — yet frogs raised in zoos are harmless, because the poison comes from what they eat in the wild.

programs.summary: Smithsonian-led partnership with Cheyenne Mountain Zoo and Zoo New England that breeds Panama's most threatened frogs at its Gamboa rescue center, studies how to blunt the chytrid fungus, and ran the 2025 golden frog release trial near El Valle.

programs.title: Project Golden Frog
programs.summary: Keeps the largest golden frog colony outside Panama — hundreds of frogs in a conservation center inside the zoo hospital, the core of the AZA Species Survival Plan — and sends staff to El Valle to build breeding tanks and plan reintroductions.
